passage: I'm Sarika, Irawati's older sister. I'm in the same school, so I saw it all last week. Megha, Irawati's best friend, came to class with a fever and her mother came to fetch her at lunch. Irawati picked up Megha's heavy bag as well as her own and carried both down three floors, red in the face. The next day some girls crowded around Irawati asking why Megha had been crying in the corridor before the fever. Irawati just said, "She wasn't feeling well." I found out later Megha had told Irawati something private about her grandmother's dog dying. Irawati never told anyone, not even me. I don't know what she was thinking, but she looked very serious about it.

qa.q: How many floors did Irawati carry both bags down?
qa.a: Three floors.

qa.q: What might Irawati have been feeling when the girls crowded around asking questions?
qa.a: She probably felt protective of Megha and determined to keep her trust, which is why she gave only a short answer and looked serious.

qa.q: What choice at the corridor showed Irawati's loyalty?
qa.a: When the girls asked why Megha was crying, Irawati chose to say only that Megha wasn't feeling well, keeping the private news safe.

qa.q: How does Sarika see Irawati's silence?
qa.a: Sarika isn't sure what Irawati was thinking, but seems impressed that Irawati kept the secret even from her own sister.

grounding: An older sister observes a child carrying a sick friend's bag and keeping a harmless secret she was trusted with.

passage: Monday: At recess, Aditi whispered to Zainab behind the water tank, "We're moving to Bhopal next month. Don't tell anyone yet, I want to tell them myself." Zainab crossed her heart. Wednesday: Aditi came to school with a bad cold and a thick scarf. Zainab carried Aditi's bag up to the classroom and back down at home time, even though her own was heavy with atlases. When Ritika asked, "Why is Aditi so quiet lately? Is something wrong?" Zainab shrugged and changed the subject to the cricket match. Friday: Aditi stood up in class and told everyone about moving. Afterwards she hugged Zainab hard. "You didn't tell. Not even Ritika." Zainab grinned. "It was yours to tell."

qa.q: Where are Aditi's family moving?
qa.a: To Bhopal, next month.

qa.q: Why did Zainab change the subject when Ritika asked about Aditi?
qa.a: Zainab wanted to protect Aditi's trust and let Aditi share the news in her own way.

qa.q: What choices across the week showed Zainab's loyalty?
qa.a: Zainab carried Aditi's bag while she was ill and kept the moving news secret until Aditi told everyone herself.

qa.q: How does Aditi feel toward Zainab by Friday?
qa.a: Aditi feels grateful and close to Zainab, hugging her hard because the secret was kept 🤗

grounding: Over a week a child carries an ill friend's bag and keeps her friend's secret until the friend chooses to share it.

passage: Ojas, you want a story? When I was ten, my best friend Bansi got jaundice and was weak for weeks. Our school was two kilometres away, over the canal bridge. Every morning I walked to his house first, took his cloth bag, and carried both of ours. My shoulders ached. My mother said, "Harish, you're not his coolie." I didn't care. Bansi was mine to look after. There was something else too. Bansi couldn't read the blackboard well yet, and he was ashamed. He asked me to whisper the words to him, and not to tell. I whispered for a whole year. I never told the teacher or the other boys. You're the first person I've told, and Bansi is ninety now, so I think he'll forgive me.

qa.q: How far away was the school?
qa.a: Two kilometres away, over the canal bridge.

qa.q: How did Harish feel about carrying both bags despite aching shoulders?
qa.a: Harish felt that Bansi was his to look after, so caring for his friend mattered more than the ache or his mother's teasing.

qa.q: What was the key choice Harish made about Bansi's reading, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Harish chose to whisper the words and keep it secret, which protected Bansi from shame while still helping him learn.

qa.q: What was it like for Bansi to have a friend like Harish?
qa.a: Bansi, weak and ashamed, had someone to carry his bag and quietly help him read, so he could keep going to school without being mocked.

grounding: An elder recalls carrying a sick friend's bag as a boy and keeping the friend's harmless secret out of loyalty.

passage:
The bus to school was cancelled because the road had flooded, so everyone in Manjula's lane had to walk the long way through the rain. Her friend Shreya had a fever, and the girl could barely keep up.
Manjula, ten, took Shreya's heavy bag without asking and hung it on her own front, so she looked like a turtle with two shells. Water splashed over her sandals. Her shoulders ached.
"You'll get tired," Shreya said weakly.
"I'm fine. Hold the umbrella."
At the school gate, Kusum's gang ran up. "Shreya, is it true you sleep with a toy rabbit? Manjula knows. Tell us, Manjula!"
Shreya had told her that on a sleepover, whispering. Manjula's face went hot. "I don't know anything," she said, and walked Shreya straight to the sick room.

qa.q: Why did everyone have to walk the long way?
qa.a: The bus to school was cancelled because the road had flooded.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling when Kusum's gang asked about the toy rabbit?
qa.a: She felt hot-faced and uncomfortable under pressure, but she was determined not to betray what Shreya had trusted her with.

qa.q: What choice did Manjula make at the school gate, and why did it matter to Shreya?
qa.a: She refused to reveal the secret and took Shreya to the sick room, protecting both Shreya's trust and her health.

qa.q: How might Shreya feel about Manjula after that walk?
qa.a: Shreya would likely feel deeply grateful and safe, knowing her friend carried her bag in the rain and kept her secret.

grounding: It shows a child who carries an ill friend's bag through the rain and keeps a secret she was trusted with, caring most strongly for someone close.

passage:
Parul came back to school after chickenpox still weak and blotchy, and her classroom in the Mumbai school was on the fourth floor. Vasudha, eleven, met her at the gate every morning that week and carried her bag up all four flights, then her own.
"You don't have to," Parul said.
"You'd do it for me."
On Thursday the school magazine came out. There was a poem about a lonely pigeon on the water tank, signed only "Anonymous." Vasudha knew. Parul had shown it to her in the library, whispering, "Don't tell anyone. I'll die."
At lunch the whole table guessed. "Vasudha, you know, don't you? Your face says so!"
Vasudha bit into her chapati and shrugged. Under the table, Parul squeezed her hand.

qa.q: What was the poem in the school magazine about?
qa.a: A lonely pigeon on the water tank.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling when the whole table pressed her at lunch?
qa.a: She felt the pressure and some nerves, since they said her face gave it away, but she held firm with a shrug to protect Parul's trust.

qa.q: What choice did Vasudha make at lunch, and what did it show Parul?
qa.a: She stayed quiet instead of revealing the poem's author, showing Parul that her trust was safe.

qa.q: What does Parul's hand squeeze suggest about how she sees Vasudha?
qa.a: It suggests Parul feels grateful and close to her, seeing Vasudha as a loyal friend who carried her bag and kept her secret.

grounding: It shows a child who carries a recovering classmate's bag every day and keeps the secret she was trusted with, caring most for someone she knows well.

passage:
Class 5 observation note, Thursday.
Aadhya came back after three days with fever and was still weak. At the end of the day I saw Vijay, ten, pick up her heavy school bag along with his own and carry both down three flights of stairs to the gate.
When I asked him, he shrugged. "She's my friend. Her bag is too heavy for fever."
Later they were whispering, and went quiet when they saw me. I asked what the secret was. Vijay said firmly, "It's Aadhya's secret, ma'am. I promised."
On Friday I found out: they had been making a birthday card for me.
What I did next: nothing, except say thank you for the card, and thank Vijay for carrying the bag.

qa.q: How many flights of stairs did Vijay carry both bags down?
qa.a: Three flights of stairs.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling when he refused to share the secret?
qa.a: He felt loyal and protective of Aadhya's trust, determined to keep his promise.

qa.q: How did the note-writer respond, and why was that wise?
qa.a: They didn't push for the secret and later just thanked both children, respecting a harmless secret and Vijay's care for his friend.

qa.q: How might Aadhya have felt when Vijay carried her bag?
qa.a: She probably felt cared for and grateful, since she was still weak after the fever.

grounding: It shows a child carrying an ill friend's bag and keeping a harmless secret she trusted him with.

passage:
Monday
Irfan still has the cough, so I carried his bag again today. Plus mine. My shoulders are dead but whatever. He'd do it for me.
At lunch he told me something and made me swear not to tell. He's really scared of the swimming test next week. Like, really scared. His hands were shaking when he said it.
Faisal asked me in the bus, "Why is Irfan so quiet?" and I said, "Cough." Which is true.
I won't tell anyone. But I told Irfan maybe he could tell Sir himself, or I'd go with him if he wanted. He said maybe.
Best friends carry your bag and keep your secrets. That's the rule.
– Imran

qa.q: Why did Imran carry Irfan's bag?
qa.a: Because Irfan still had the cough.

qa.q: How does Imran feel about keeping Irfan's secret?
qa.a: Imran feels loyal and protective, determined not to tell anyone what Irfan shared.

qa.q: What did Imran suggest, and why is it a good idea?
qa.a: Imran suggested Irfan tell Sir himself, with Imran going along, so an adult could help with the fear while the secret stays Irfan's to share.

qa.q: How might Irfan feel about Imran's loyalty?
qa.a: He probably feels safe and trusted, knowing his friend helps him and keeps his fear private.

grounding: It shows a child carrying an ill friend's bag and keeping a secret he was trusted with.

passage:
On the mud road home from the village school, Urmila, nine, carried two bags: hers on her back, and Ojas's in her arms. Ojas walked beside her, flushed with fever, coughing.
"I can carry it," he croaked.
"No, you can't," Urmila said. "You're sick."
At the well, he stopped. "Urmila, don't tell anyone about the tin."
She knew about the tin. For two months he'd been saving his coins from errands in an old tea tin, to buy his mother a sari for her birthday.
"I won't," she said. She had already been asked twice by his sister what he was hiding.
At his door she handed him the bag. "Get better. And keep saving."

qa.q: What was Ojas saving for?
qa.a: To buy his mother a sari for her birthday.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling as she carried both bags?
qa.a: She felt protective and caring towards her sick friend, determined to help him.

qa.q: How could an adult support what Urmila is doing?
qa.a: An adult could praise her help and respect the harmless secret, since loyalty to friends is a strong good at this age.

qa.q: How might Ojas's mother feel when she gets the sari?
qa.a: She would probably feel surprised and moved, knowing he saved for months.

grounding: It shows a child carrying an ill friend's bag and keeping his secret about a birthday surprise.

passage:
Selin had a fever but insisted on coming to school in Istanbul for the class trip photo. By noon she was pale and slow.
Gabriel, ten, took her heavy backpack without asking and carried it on his front, with his own on his back, all the way to her bus stop.
"You look like a turtle," Selin croaked.
"A strong turtle."
At the stop she whispered, "Don't tell anyone I cried in the toilet. I was just tired."
"I won't."
The next day Emre asked, "Was Selin crying yesterday?" Gabriel shrugged. "She was sick. That's all." He kept his promise, even though Emre looked at him strangely.

qa.q: How did Gabriel carry Selin's backpack?
qa.a: He carried it on his front, with his own on his back.

qa.q: Why did Gabriel keep Selin's secret even when Emre asked?
qa.a: He felt loyal and protective toward his friend, and wanted her to trust him, so keeping his promise mattered to him.

qa.q: What does Gabriel's help show about caring for close friends?
qa.a: Small practical acts like carrying a bag and keeping a harmless secret show strong loyalty and care.

qa.q: How might Selin feel when she hears Gabriel kept her secret?
qa.a: Selin would likely feel relieved and grateful, trusting him even more.

grounding: A child carries an ill classmate's bag and keeps her harmless secret, showing loyal care for a close friend.

passage:
At the Class 5 annual day rehearsal in a Mysuru school, Lavanya sprained her ankle and had to use a crutch. Chinmay, her neighbour since babyhood, carried her school bag, her water bottle and her costume box from room to room.
"You don't have to," Lavanya said.
"I want to."
In the costume room, she whispered, "Don't tell anyone I'm scared of the stage. I'm pretending my ankle is why I'm nervous."
Chinmay nodded. When the dance teacher asked him why Lavanya looked worried, he said, "Her ankle hurts, Ma'am." Later, he stood near the wings for her dance, making silly faces so she'd laugh instead of freeze.

qa.q: What did Chinmay carry for Lavanya?
qa.a: He carried her school bag, her water bottle and her costume box.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling as he carried Lavanya's things?
qa.a: He felt caring and loyal toward his old friend, wanting to help her because she mattered to him.

qa.q: How could Chinmay support Lavanya's stage fear beyond keeping the secret?
qa.a: He can keep cheering her from the wings, and gently encourage her to tell the teacher when she is ready, since it's a harmless worry.

qa.q: How might Lavanya feel seeing Chinmay's silly faces in the wings?
qa.a: She would probably feel safer and less alone, able to laugh instead of freezing.

grounding: A child carries an injured friend's things and keeps her harmless secret, showing loyalty to those close to him.

passage:
Monday: Sachin came to school with a bandaged wrist after falling off his cycle. Mohit, his best friend, picked up Sachin's bag and carried it to Class 6.
Wednesday: Mohit was still carrying the bag, and fetched Sachin's lunch from the canteen. At lunch Sachin whispered, "Don't tell anyone, but I fell because I was trying to show off a no-hands trick." Mohit promised.
Friday: Some boys teased, "Sachin fell like a baby!" Mohit didn't tell them the real reason. He just said, "Anyone can fall," and sat next to Sachin. Walking home, Sachin said, "You're the best." Mohit grinned. "I know."

qa.q: Why did Sachin come to school with a bandaged wrist?
qa.a: He had fallen off his cycle.

qa.q: Why did Mohit keep Sachin's secret when the boys teased?
qa.a: He felt loyal and protective of his best friend, and didn't want Sachin embarrassed.

qa.q: What is a kind way Mohit handled the teasing?
qa.a: He didn't join in or share the secret; he said anyone can fall and sat next to Sachin.

qa.q: How might Sachin feel about Mohit's help that week?
qa.a: He probably feels grateful and close to Mohit, trusting him even more.

grounding: Over a week, a child carries his injured friend's bag and keeps his embarrassing secret, showing loyalty within his circle.

passage: Hrithik, you ask why I still visit Savitri every Makar Sankranti. Sit, I'll tell you. I was ten, and that January kites filled the sky, but Savitri came back to school thin as a stick after a long fever. Her satchel was heavy with slates and books, so every day I carried it, mine on my back and hers in my arms, all the way to her lane. One evening she whispered that her father had lost his job at the mill and there was no money for kite string that year. 'Don't tell anyone, Nikita.' I didn't. Not the other girls, not even my own mother. On festival morning I just gave her half my string and said I had too much. Fifty years later she still laughs about my 'too much'.

qa.q: What did Nikita carry every day while Savitri was weak?
qa.a: Savitri's heavy satchel, carried all the way to Savitri's lane.

qa.q: Why did Nikita keep Savitri's news from everyone, even at home?
qa.a: Nikita felt loyal and protective towards Savitri, who had trusted Nikita with something painful, and that trust mattered more than talking.

qa.q: Nikita gave Savitri half the kite string and claimed to have too much. Why was that a good choice?
qa.a: It let Savitri join the festival without being pitied, and it kept the secret safe because nobody needed to know why.

qa.q: How might Savitri have felt about Nikita's 'too much' story?
qa.a: Savitri probably felt grateful and relieved not to be pitied; that is why she still laughs about it fifty years later.

grounding: An elder recalls a childhood of carrying Savitri's bag during illness and keeping her private worry, loyalty to someone close.

passage: The monsoon had turned the school path into a brown stream, and the bus was not running. Indu was still weak after a week of fever, so Anand slung her bag over his own and held the umbrella over both of them. His shoes filled with water. Twice he slipped; twice he kept the bags dry against his chest. At the corner shop Indu stopped to catch her breath. 'Don't tell the others I cried in the sick room today,' she said. 'I've missed so much work.' 'I won't,' Anand said. Next morning, when a classmate asked why Indu's eyes had been red, Anand shrugged. 'Rain gets in your eyes,' he said, and changed the subject to cricket.

qa.q: What did Anand hold over both of them?
qa.a: He held the umbrella over both of them.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling when a classmate asked about Indu's red eyes?
qa.a: He felt protective of Indu and determined to keep his promise, so he brushed the question off lightly.

qa.q: What else could Anand do if Indu stays very upset about missed work?
qa.a: He could share his notes and suggest she talk to the class teacher, while still keeping what she told him private.

qa.q: What is it like for Indu to have Anand beside her this week?
qa.a: She can lean on him while she is weak and trust him with something embarrassing, which likely makes her feel safer and less alone.

grounding: A boy carries an ill classmate's bag through the rain and keeps the secret she trusted him with.

passage: Two days before the Durga Puja holidays, the Kolkata lane outside school smelt of fresh paint from the pandal going up. Saurabh coughed all through the last period, his nose red. When the bell rang, Dilnaz picked up his bag before he could. 'I can carry it,' he croaked. 'You carry your cough,' she said. Walking past the half-built pandal, he told her very quietly that the poem about the goddess's eyes in the school puja magazine was his, printed under a made-up name. 'Nobody knows. They'd tease me.' At the gate their friends were guessing who had written it. Dilnaz only smiled, and handed Saurabh his bag at his door.

qa.q: What did Saurabh tell Dilnaz on the walk?
qa.a: That the poem about the goddess's eyes in the school puja magazine was his, printed under a made-up name.

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz only smile while the others were guessing?
qa.a: She felt loyal to Saurabh and quietly proud to be trusted, so keeping his secret mattered more than joining the guessing game.

qa.q: How could Dilnaz respond if teasing about the poem started anyway?
qa.a: She could stay by Saurabh's side and change the subject, leaving the choice to share it with him instead of revealing it herself.

qa.q: How might Saurabh feel about Dilnaz after that day?
qa.a: He likely feels grateful and safe with her, since she helped while he was ill and kept the very thing he feared being teased about.

grounding: A girl carries her coughing friend's bag and keeps his secret, caring for someone she knows well.

passage:
"Gargi, you're shivering," Francis said at the classroom door. "Give me your bag."
"It's heavy. My rangoli colours are in it."
"I carry my cricket kit every day. Give."
He slung both bags on, one on each shoulder, and walked her to the auto.
At the gate, Rohit caught up. "What's her rangoli design for the Diwali contest? You know, na? Tell."
"She told me because she trusts me," Francis said.
"Just a hint!"
"Nope."
"Boring."
"Fine. Boring." Francis waved as the auto pulled away. "Get well, Gargi! Your design's locked up safe."
Gargi smiled weakly from the seat. "Knew it would be."

qa.q: What was in Gargi's heavy bag?
qa.a: Her rangoli colours.

qa.q: Why does Francis refuse to give Rohit even a hint?
qa.a: Francis feels loyal and protective of Gargi's trust, since she told him because she trusts him.

qa.q: What would you tell a child pressed to share a friend's surprise like this one?
qa.a: Keeping a harmless surprise, like a rangoli design, is a kind way to honour trust; a secret about someone being hurt, though, should always go to a trusted adult.

qa.q: How might Gargi feel watching Francis from the auto?
qa.a: Gargi, shivering and unwell, likely felt cared for and safe, knowing her bag and her design were in good hands.

grounding: A child carries an ill classmate's bag and keeps the harmless surprise she trusted him with.
